cim_eredeti: PODCAST | The Real-World Application of Artificial Intelligence in Manufacturing
szoveg_eredeti:
Dr. Linir Zamir, who’s been working on the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite, discusses how Artificial Intelligence is re-shaping manufacturing. AI is moving fast, and on the factory floor, that speed brings both excitement and real concern. Some workers worry it’s going to replace them. Others are interested, but hesitant, because they’ve heard about hallucinations, bad outputs and AI tools that sound great in theory but fall apart in real operations. In this conversation, we focus on the practical side: how people in the AI industry are working to make these systems more reliable, how manufacturers can use AI to strengthen the workforce they already have and what it actually looks like to deploy AI across the factory floor in a way that delivers return on investment.

ASSEMBLY: Folks are fearful of AI taking over their jobs. From your perspective, what’s the most realistic way workers should think about AI? And what advice would you give to someone who’s worried it’s going to replace them?

Listen to our interview with Dr. Linir Zamir!

ZAMIR: It makes sense to be cautious about AI. I understand it. You hear it all over. You’ve seen the movies, and the idea of AI can be terrifying sometimes. But I think nowadays, as time progresses and we see more and more AI evolving within our daily lives—like ChatGPT—people are now using it for almost anything, even drafting an email. You can use ChatGPT. ChatGPT does not send the email, but it does help you draft a better version of it. That’s exactly the same way we think about agents in manufacturing. We’re not replacing the operator. We’re not taking the job from them. We’re giving the operator the tools to make better decisions, to understand the procedure better, and to have the right context whenever they need it. Every evolution has some cautiousness and fearfulness related to it, and it’s the same with AI. But it’s something that the more we understand, the less we’re afraid of it. We’re giving the operators—and any level of the manufacturer—the tools, but we also explain how the tool behaves. What exactly does it do? What data is being transferred between the different agents? So we don’t give just the tool by itself, but also a deeper understanding of what exactly is happening, so people can understand it and not be afraid of it. And yeah. At the end of the day, we are not replacing; we are enhancing.

ASSEMBLY: In the recent past, AI has been criticized for a number of reasons. How do folks in the AI industry tackle these issues to make sure the AI agents are as foolproof as they can be?

ZAMIR: I think there are two points to what you said. One of them is that up until recently, AI had the issue of what is called hallucination, where it was not as reliable. People found errors or issues. There was a famous example with ChatGPT and the number of “R’s” in the word “strawberry.” I don’t know if you’ve heard of that, but ChatGPT hallucinated 30% to 40% of the time. If we are trying to build agents for manufacturers, where every second counts and accuracy is critical, we cannot allow those hallucinations. But in the past year or so, we’ve seen tools—and the foundation models themselves—become as reliable as you can get, assuming you give them the right context, which is what we do with the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite. We provide the right context. And there’s going to be pushback on any new technology.

ASSEMBLY: That’s a very good point about pushback. How do you handle that when you talk to manufacturers?

ZAMIR: First of all, the quality of the language models is much better than it used to be. We are in a very close relationship with NVIDIA, as mentioned, and we are implementing some foundation models. For example, Cosmos. Cosmos is a foundation model that is designed to be specific for manufacturing, so it has a much better understanding of the environment. That’s one thing. But hallucination depends on the context that you provide to the agent, because deviceWISE has so much data. So for any question or any understanding the agent needs, we provide the proper context. And we also have MCP protocol, which allows us to provide the agents with exactly the right context they need in order to understand, make a decision, and provide the right result or output to the operator for any input it might get. Those are the ways we can essentially fix, or handle, cases of hallucination. I would say this is 99.9% hallucination-proof, but for the 0.01%, that’s why you still have the person. That’s why we still need the person to validate and to say, “That’s true,” or “Holds up. It’s not an issue like you think it is.” But having this person is a layer of protection. The longer you have the agent running, and the longer it can interact with a person and understand the context of the environment it resides in, the less chance there is of it making any mistake or hallucination. So yeah: the quality of the agent, the MCP or the context involved, and then the person at the end to verify that everything is accurate. That’s part of it. Like all agentic AI, there’s going to be pushback, but the way we solve that and make people believe in the technology is to show them. We are comfortable with what we bring. We know what we have, and we’ve seen success all around. Being able to put the technology on the factory floor—bringing the small hardware component that can suddenly see everything—and showing them, “Hey, listen, within a minute I can see all the temperature changes, and I can give you an evaluation of what might fault within the next week or month,” and giving them this data shows the value. Initially, they might push back a little, but once they see the results they expect to see, it becomes much easier to adopt those technologies. At the end of the day, it’s a question of money, like almost everything is. If we can help manufacturers lower cost and lower downtime—which costs them a lot of money—they will definitely be inclined to adopt that technology and use the new tools that are available nowadays.

ASSEMBLY: A lot of manufacturers, because of the skilled labor shortage, are having to take the teams that they already have and make the most of them. This idea of using AI to enhance the operator basically means giving the people on the plant floor tools that help them work faster, make better decisions, and solve problems more consistently, without replacing their expertise or taking them out of the process, right?

ZAMIR: Yeah, definitely. And what you said, we’ve heard so many times before. Actually, even NVIDIA themselves brought this up the other day when we had a conversation with them.

ASSEMBLY: Can you explain how AI programs like the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite fit into this idea?

ZAMIR: The Intelligence Suite helps exactly with that situation. We can take the operator, and we can even help with the training of an operator. Instead of spending hours and taking time from other operators to teach or explain, you can have the Intelligence Suite as the source of knowledge that every operator can use to know more and to understand the process that needs to be taken, to be much more productive, to understand the concept of the factory much better, and to know exactly what steps need to be taken. So we definitely help with that specific issue that we’ve seen across all factories that we’ve worked with.
